name: parted
summary: Creates, deletes and changes the partitions of a disk.
description: GNU Parted edits a disk’s partition table: it can create a new table (GPT or msdos), and add, delete, resize or rename partitions. Run with just a disk, it opens an interactive mode (“(parted)” prompt). With commands after the disk, it runs them one after the other then quits; the -s (--script) option then suppresses every confirmation question. Positions are written with a unit (MiB, GiB, MB…) or as a percentage of the disk (0% = start, 100% = end). Watch out: parted writes changes immediately, with no “save” step. It does not format partitions: use mkfs afterwards.

options.description: Shows the partition table of every disk, then quits.

example.output:
Model: ATA Samsung SSD 870 (scsi)
Disk /dev/sda: 500GB
Partition Table: gpt

Number  Start   End    Size   File system  Name  Flags
 1      1049kB  538MB  537MB  fat32        boot  boot, esp
 2      538MB   500GB  500GB  ext4         root

options.description: Script mode: shows no confirmation questions (“Yes/No?”). Essential for chaining commands unattended, but parted will not ask whether you are sure you want to wipe the disk.
Alignment rule for new partitions on the disk’s physical blocks (optimal by default, recommended for performance).
In script mode, automatically answers “Fix” to problems detected (a misplaced backup GPT table, for example).
Shows help and the list of commands.

arguments.name: DISK
arguments.description: The whole disk to change: /dev/sda, /dev/sdb, /dev/nvme0n1… (not a partition like /dev/sda1). “sdX” is an example to replace with the disk’s real letter, shown by lsblk or parted -l.

subcommands.name: mklabel
subcommands.description: Creates a new, empty partition table on the disk. All existing partitions disappear: their data becomes inaccessible.

arguments.name: TABLE-TYPE
arguments.description: Table type: gpt (modern, disks over 2 TB, up to 128 partitions, required for UEFI boot) or msdos (old MBR format: 4 primary partitions, 2 TB maximum).

subcommands.name: mkpart
subcommands.description: Creates a partition in free space, between a start position and an end position. It is not formatted: you will then need to create a file system (mkfs.ext4, mkfs.fat…).

arguments.name: NAME
arguments.description: On a GPT table: the partition’s name (label), free text, for example “boot” or “system”. On an msdos table, you give its type instead (primary, logical or extended), optionally followed by a file system (ext4, fat32…) that is only a hint.

arguments.name: START
arguments.description: Where the partition starts. As a percentage of the disk (0% = right at the start, parted then leaves the alignment space needed) or with a unit: 500MiB = 500 mebibytes (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes), 1GiB, 20GB… Without a unit, parted counts in megabytes (MB).

arguments.name: END
arguments.description: Where the partition ends, same format as the start. 100% = up to the end of the disk. To chain two partitions with no gap, the end of one is the start of the next (500MiB then 500MiB).

subcommands.name: print
subcommands.description: Shows the disk’s partition table: numbers, start, end, size, file system, name and flags.

subcommands.name: rm
subcommands.description: Deletes a partition (and makes its data inaccessible).

arguments.name: NUMBER
arguments.description: Partition number, as shown by print (1, 2…).

subcommands.name: set
subcommands.description: Turns a flag on or off on a partition.

arguments.name: NUMBER
arguments.description: Partition number, as shown by print.

arguments.name: FLAG
arguments.description: Flag to change: boot (boot partition), esp (EFI system partition), lvm, raid, swap, bios_grub, hidden…

arguments.name: STATE
arguments.description: on to turn the flag on, off to remove it.

subcommands.name: name
subcommands.description: Changes the name of a partition (GPT tables only).

arguments.name: NUMBER
arguments.description: Number of the partition to rename.

subcommands.name: resizepart
subcommands.description: Moves the end of a partition to grow or shrink it. The file system inside is not resized (resize2fs for ext4).

arguments.name: NUMBER
arguments.description: Number of the partition to resize.

subcommands.name: unit
subcommands.description: Chooses the unit used to show and enter positions.

arguments.name: UNIT
arguments.description: s (sectors), B, kB, MB, GB, MiB, GiB, % or compact.

subcommands.name: align-check
subcommands.description: Checks that a partition is aligned on the disk’s physical blocks.

arguments.name: NUMBER
arguments.description: Number of the partition to check.

examples.explanation: Shows the disk’s partitions, without changing anything.
examples.output:
Disk /dev/sda: 500GB
Partition Table: gpt

Number  Start   End    Size   File system  Name  Flags
 1      1049kB  538MB  537MB  fat32        boot  boot, esp
 2      538MB   500GB  500GB  ext4         root

examples.command: sudo parted /dev/sdX -s mklabel gpt mkpart "boot_partition_name" 0% 500MiB mkpart "system_partition_name" 500MiB 100%
examples.explanation: With no questions at all: wipes the table of disk sdX, creates a GPT table, a 500 MiB boot partition at the start, then a system partition taking up all the rest.
Replaces sdb’s partition table with an empty msdos (MBR) table.
Turns on the boot flag on partition 1.
Grows partition 2 up to the end of the disk.
Shows the table while automatically fixing a misplaced backup GPT table (after cloning a disk onto a bigger one, for example).
Interactive mode: type print, mkpart… at the (parted) prompt, then quit.

dangerNote: parted applies each change immediately. mklabel and rm make the disk’s data inaccessible, and with -s no confirmation is asked. Check the disk name with lsblk or parted -l: getting the letter wrong (sda instead of sdb) can wipe your system.
